- LNG project expected to unlock 47.13 trillion cubic feet of natural gas reserves
- Tanzania aims to double power generation capacity to 8,000 megawatts by 2030, minister says
- Government expected to decide by June whether to seek new IMF ​lending programme

LONDON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Tanzania expects to finalise agreements on major ‌investment projects in the coming months, including a $42 billion LNG development that officials hope will underpin industrialisation, Finance Minister Khamis Mussa Omar told Reuters.

The liquefied natural gas project — led by Equinor [(EQNR.OL), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/EQNR.OL) and Shell [(SHEL.L), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/SHEL.L) — is part of a broader effort to establish East Africa ​as a major energy hub, alongside Uganda's planned first oil exports via the Tanzanian port of ​Tanga in early 2027.

It is expected to unlock 47.13 trillion cubic feet of natural gas ⁠reserves. Exxon Mobil [(XOM.N), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/XOM.N), Pavilion Energy, Medco Energi [(MEDC.JK), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/MEDC.JK) and state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation are also partners.

Officials had expected ​the LNG agreement to be signed before June.

"It's almost there," Omar said.

Equinor and Shell did not respond to a ​request for comment.

While most LNG will be exported, part of the production will be for the domestic market.

## CRITICAL MINERALS PROJECT DEALS

Omar said Tanzania aims to roughly double power generation capacity to 8,000 megawatts by 2030 while increasing the share of energy from sources ​the government classifies as clean, including hydropower, solar, wind and natural gas, to around 75%.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

He said agreements on ​two critical mineral projects were also close, declining to provide details, but adding that US investors in particular are drawn to ‌energy ⁠and critical mineral projects.

Tanzania is seeking more international investment in projects that are set to generate revenue and help finance themselves, he said.

The government has yet to decide whether to issue an international bond, but is working to attract foreign investors to domestic debt.

Tanzania widened foreign investor access to its domestic bond market in July, launched a sovereign ​yield curve in August ​and enacted reforms to ⁠boost corporate debt issuance. However, it is still assessing the risks of greater foreign participation, Omar said, adding that the central bank is studying the experience of other ​African countries.

The move mirrors a broader trend across [frontier markets](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/angola-moves-open-local-bond-market-eyes-jpmorgan-debt-benchmark-2026-09-09/) to tap global demand for [local-currency ​debt](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/jpmorgan-launch-frontier-market-local-currency-debt-index-by-month-end-source-2026-09-14/).

Tanzania now funds ⁠two-thirds of its roughly 62.3 trillion Tanzanian shillings ($23.7 billion) budget via domestic revenue. Official development assistance, which once accounted for 40% of the budget, is falling globally and now accounts for a "very, very negligible" share, Omar said.

The government is ⁠also assessing ​whether to seek a new IMF lending programme and expects to ​decide by June, he said.

Tanzania's previous $1.7 billion IMF programme, including an Extended Credit Facility and a climate-focused Resilience and Sustainability Facility, concluded in ​July.

($1 = 2,625.0000 Tanzanian shillings)
